cards.front: An {{c1::adaptation}} is an inherited trait that helps survival and reproduction in a particular ecosystem.
cards.quote: An adaptation is an inherited trait that helps survival and reproduction in a particular ecosystem.

cards.front: A {{c1::physical adaptation}} is a feature of the body: a body covering, a color, or a structure.
cards.quote: A physical adaptation is a feature of the body: a body covering, a color, or a structure.

cards.front: A {{c1::behavioral adaptation}} is an action or a pattern of actions.
cards.quote: A behavioral adaptation is an action or a pattern of actions.

cards.front: The snowshoe hare's white winter coat is {{c1::camouflage}}, coloring that helps an animal blend into its background.
cards.quote: The hare's white coat is camouflage, coloring that helps an animal blend into its background.

cards.front: {{c1::Migration}} is a regular journey between places used in different seasons.
cards.back: Example: monarch butterflies flying south in fall.
cards.quote: Migration is a regular journey between places used in different seasons.

cards.front: A {{c1::population}} is all the members of one species in one area.
cards.quote: A population is all the members of one species in one area.

cards.front: Why is a groundhog's hibernation counted as both a behavior and a change in how the body works?
cards.back: Going into a burrow and staying inactive is the behavior. Inside, the heart beats much more slowly and the body cools, which is a change in how the body works.
cards.quote: Inside, the groundhog's heart beats much more slowly and its body cools, which is a change in how the body works.

cards.front: A student says, "The hare turned white because it needed to hide." What is wrong with that explanation?
cards.back: A hare cannot choose a new coat. Its molt follows a yearly schedule, and day length seems to help set that schedule.
cards.quote: Variation is a difference between hares, not a change inside one hare: a hare cannot choose a new coat, because its molt follows a yearly schedule.

cards.front: What is a trade-off in an adaptation? Give an example using the hare's white coat.
cards.back: A trade-off is a trait that helps in one way but costs in another. The white coat hides a hare on snow but makes it stand out on bare ground.
cards.why: A trade-off is not a failure; no living thing is perfectly adapted.
cards.quote: A trade-off is not a failure; no living thing is perfectly adapted.

cards.front: What does variation mean, and what did Montana hares show about it?
cards.back: Variation means differences among individuals of a species. Some Montana hares turned white earlier than others.
cards.quote: In Montana, some hares turned white earlier than others.

cards.front: A bird's beak works a bit like a tool. Where does that comparison break down?
cards.back: A person can put a tool down or pick up a different one, but a bird cannot swap its beak.
cards.quote: You can put a tool down or pick up a different one, but a bird cannot swap its beak.

cards.front: What helps set when a snowshoe hare changes coat, and why does that cause trouble when snow melts early?
cards.back: Day length seems to help set the schedule. Snow can shift spring timing somewhat, but not enough to keep every Montana hare matched to the ground.
cards.quote: Snow can shift spring timing somewhat, but not enough to keep every Montana hare matched.

cards.front: In this lesson, what does "population change" mean, and what does it not mean?
cards.back: It means inherited traits become more or less common in a population. It does not mean that an individual never learns, grows or responds.
cards.quote: Population change means that inherited traits become more or less common.

cards.front: In a Montana forest the snow melts two weeks early, but the hares change color at the usual time. Which hares are most likely to be spotted by predators, and why?
cards.back: White hares on bare brown ground. Their coat no longer matches the ground, so it stands out.
cards.quote: When snow melts early, a white hare stands out on brown ground, and in Montana mismatched hares had a lower estimated chance of surviving each week.

cards.front: A Montana study estimated a one-week survival chance of 96 percent for matched hares and 89 percent for fully mismatched hares. What is the difference in percentage points, and about how many of 100 hares in each group survive the week?
cards.back: 96 - 89 = 7 percentage points. About 96 matched and 89 fully mismatched hares survive out of 100.
cards.quote: Out of 100, the estimates give about 96 matched survivors and 89 fully mismatched survivors.
cards.section: Survival of matched and mismatched hares

cards.front: Clay mice on light sand: dark 5 attacks, light 2. On dark soil: light 16, dark 5. What fraction of all attacks hit models that did not match the ground?
cards.back: Mismatched models: 5 + 16 = 21. All attacks: 5 + 2 + 16 + 5 = 28. 21/28 = three out of four.
cards.quote: Mismatched models (dark on sand, light on soil) received 5 + 16 = 21 of 28 attacks, or three out of four.
cards.section: Survival of matched and mismatched hares

cards.front: A cardinal has a short, thick beak that cracks seeds. Is this a physical or behavioral adaptation, and what does it help the bird get?
cards.back: Physical, because the beak is a structure of the body. It helps the bird get food (seeds).
cards.quote: A cardinal's short, thick beak cracks seeds.

cards.front: Using the Montana estimate of an 89 percent weekly survival chance for fully mismatched hares, about how many of 200 such hares would you expect to survive a week? Does this tell you which hares will die?
cards.back: About 178 (0.89 x 200). No. It is an expectation for a group, not a promise about any one hare.
cards.quote: This is an expectation for groups, not a promise about any one hare.
cards.section: Survival of matched and mismatched hares

cards.front: On dark inland soil in Florida, light clay models had 16 attacks and dark models had 5. About how many times more attacks did the mismatched models receive?
cards.back: 16 / 5 = 3.2, so about three times as many attacks on the light (mismatched) models.
cards.quote: Models sat out in the field at Topsail Hill Preserve State Park (beach) and at an inland site, in Florida.
cards.section: Survival of matched and mismatched hares

cards.front: A class tests camouflage with white and brown paper squares on a white sheet and then a brown sheet, and classmates pick up squares. What are the independent and dependent variables, and what result supports camouflage?
cards.back: Independent variable: whether a square matches the background. Dependent variable: the number of each color picked up. If matching squares are picked up less on both backgrounds, the result supports camouflage.
cards.quote: If matching squares are picked up less on both backgrounds, the result supports camouflage.

cards.front: Winters get shorter, so snow melts earlier each year. Why can individual hares not fix their mismatch, and what must happen for the timing of the population to shift?
cards.back: An individual's molt follows a yearly schedule it cannot choose; snow shifts spring timing only somewhat. A lasting change in timing can happen only across generations, if hares vary in an inherited way and some leave more young.
cards.quote: A lasting change in timing can happen only across generations, if hares vary in an inherited way and some leave more young.

cards.front: Why does the clay mouse study add to the hare survival estimates as evidence that color affects survival?
cards.back: The clay mouse study tested color directly by setting light and dark models on light and dark ground, and mismatched models had more attacks. The hare numbers are rounded model estimates; the clay mouse counts test color directly.
cards.quote: A second team tested color directly with clay mice.
cards.section: Survival of matched and mismatched hares
